Many monarchs from eastern North America migrate thousands of miles to mountain forests in central Mexico, where they spend the winter in enormous colonies. The round trip spans several generations. It often hunts by doing almost nothing: standing motionless in shallow water until a fish comes within striking distance. During breeding season, adults grow long ornamental plumes on the back. Demand for those feathers in the hat trade devastated egret populations in the late 1800s and helped spur some of America's earliest bird-protection campaigns. Great Egrets nest in colonies, building stick nests in trees and shrubs, often over water and alongside other herons and egrets.

quick: A Common Gallinule is a dark marsh bird with a bright red forehead shield, a red-and-yellow bill and a white stripe along each side. It swims like a duck but has no webbing on its feet. The Common Gallinule belongs to the rail family. Very long toes spread its weight across soft mud and floating vegetation, letting the bird walk where a web-footed duck would push through. Gallinules are often heard before they are seen, giving loud clucks, squawks and whinnying calls from dense pond vegetation.

quick: A flock of white birds walking across wet grass with long downcurved reddish bills is usually a flock of White Ibises. Young White Ibises are brown and white rather than all white. Their adult plumage and bright red-pink bare parts develop gradually. The curved bill is a sensitive probe. An ibis pushes it into mud or soft ground and closes it when it feels a crayfish, crab, insect or other prey. White Ibises nest in colonies in trees, shrubs and sometimes dense marsh vegetation, often alongside other wading birds.

quick: An Anhinga often swims with its body submerged and only the long snakelike neck above water, which is why it is called the snakebird. Its feathers become waterlogged more easily than those of most waterbirds. Combined with dense bones, that reduces buoyancy and helps the bird slip below the surface to hunt. Underwater, an Anhinga stalks fish and drives its sharp bill through the side of the prey with a rapid thrust. After fishing, Anhingas often perch with their wings spread, drying waterlogged feathers before flying again.

quick: A small brown lizard doing push-ups on a fence or low tree trunk is often a Brown Anole. It is native to the Caribbean, not Florida, and is now widespread across the state. Where Brown Anoles become common, native Green Anoles often shift upward into shrubs and trees. Experiments have shown that Green Anole populations pushed onto higher, narrower perches can evolve larger toepads within only a few generations.
